content:
Facts: Two siblings disputed the distribution of their deceased father’s estate. The plaintiff sought reduction of a testamentary disposition allegedly infringing his reserved share, while the defendant counterclaimed for reimbursement of expenses incurred in managing and improving the inherited property. The estate consisted of several apartments devolved partly by will and partly by intestate succession.
Legal framework
Articles 536 ff. ICC on forced heirs and legitime; Article 2697 ICC on the burden of proof; Articles 1100 ff. ICC on co-ownership; principles on the action for reduction and on reimbursement of expenses in joint inheritance as developed by Supreme Court case law.
Interpretative issue
Whether a forced heir bringing an action for reduction must specifically allege and prove the existence and extent of the infringement of the reserved share, including the composition of the entire estate, and whether a co-heir may autonomously claim reimbursement of expenses outside division proceedings.
Principle applied
The forced heir who seeks reduction bears the full burden of alleging and proving all factual elements necessary to ascertain whether, and to what extent, the legitime has been infringed, including the value and composition of the entire estate and the absence of other assets capable of satisfying the reserved share. Failure to discharge this burden leads to rejection of the claim. Moreover, a co-heir who has incurred expenses for the common property may claim reimbursement only within division and accounting proceedings, not by an autonomous claim against other co-heirs; Article 1150 ICC is inapplicable in the context of joint inheritance. Both the main claim and the counterclaim were therefore rejected.
